articles.body: Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro traded personal attacks in a heated presidential debate on Sunday, a week before a closely contested runoff. The rivals accused each other of lying and corruption while clashing over the economy, security and healthcare ahead of the October 25 vote.
articles.headline: Brazil's Lula, Bolsonaro clash in bitter debate ahead of election runoff

articles.body: A year after thieves stole $100 million worth of crown jewels from Paris’s Louvre Museum, four suspects remain jailed awaiting trial, but the treasures are still missing. The October 19 heist saw thieves disguised as workers steal eight historic items, including jewellery belonging to Empress Eugenie, Napoleon III’s wife.
articles.headline: Louvre's $100 million crown jewels still missing one year after daring heist

Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that at least 19 patients were in critical condition, with some suffering severe burns requiring prolonged intensive treatment.
articles.headline: Canadian military base fire kills at least four, injures dozens

The talks came as both sides exchanged attacks on energy infrastructure, while Washington’s easing of Russian sanctions raised concerns among European allies.

articles.body: EDINBURG, Texas — A man walks out to a packed arena filled with fervent fans. Nostalgic music blasts out over the speakers as the audience of the spectacle sways and sing along. Firehouse-red campaign hats litter the heads of the devotees jammed in tight to see the show. But this isn’t a MAGA rally, and that’s not Donald Trump hitting the stage. On stage is Bobby Pulido, the Tejano star turned Democratic House candidate clad in head-to-toe leather and a black cowboy hat. The occasion? “La Ultima Desvelada,” what he said will be his final concert in Edinburg on Saturday night. Pulido is trying to flip a district that has steadily, over the past decade, slipped from the grasp of the Democratic Party and became the ultimate swing test for the country’s most culturally conservative Latino voters. If Pulido wins in Texas’ 15th District against incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz, the Democratic Party stands to gain much more than just a seat that could make a House majority. As the party looks to rebuild with Latinos and lay the groundwork for 2028, the Tejano crooner could become a strong messenger to one of Democrats’ weakest voting blocs. “Mexican-American men haven't really felt like they have a home,” in either party, Pulido told POLITICO in an interview. “It almost feels like the Latino man wants to be that provider, and he can’t fulfill that right now.” Like many Democrats this cycle, Pulido has dialed in on affordability and an aggressive economic messaging slamming Trump’s tariffs, the war with Iran and the growing stream of big corporate money in political campaigns. But unlike his fellow Democrats, Pulido echoes a social conservatism that has defined the region. He’s “ chapado a la antigua,” he told reporters Friday — a Spanish saying for old-school or traditional. “Those traditions of how [Latino men] were raised are going away, and I think there’s a lot of frustration,” Pulido told POLITICO. “They want somebody to talk to them in the language of, ‘Let me go out there and work, right? So I can provide for my family.’” Pulido has tapped into a level of political fervor and cultural star power for which the Democratic Party has been starved. Trump won the district by a staggering 18 points in 2024 — and it was redrawn by Republicans last year. But Pulido’s near-universal name ID as an Edinburg native and music star, combined with historic headwinds buffeting, put the south Texas district on the map as one of the biggest toss-ups this cycle. With just over two weeks to go, Pulido is in a dead heat against De La Cruz. He’s leaving behind three decades as a musician, multiple Latin Grammys and packed arenas for a shot at representing his hometown in the halls of Congress. The 956 region knows Pulido and his family to an extent that very few would-be members of Congress could boast. They know his father, Roberto Pulido, also a famous Tejano singer who joined his son onstage. They know his uncle, a former county judge. But beyond that, with billions of streams to his name, Pulido’s 90s hits became a ubiquitous sound for the RGV. And only in the RGV would his supporters trot up to the arena on horseback, coming off the nearby expressway. That fame, and his deep district ties, made Pulido one of the party’s most prized recruits this cycle. He’s one of the DCCC’s top candidates, with a campaign staffed in part by blue dog organizations like The Bench while also boasting the same Latino consultants as Sen. Ruben Gallego’s (D-Ariz.) 2024 Senate campaign. And Democrats see the potential for the kind of surrogate Pulido could become on the 2028 campaign trail. Many of the party’s biggest Latino voices — and attention grabbers — are further on the left. “What we haven't had is someone like Bobby Pulido, who's going to come from the moderate wing of the party, that is going to be a rock star,” Gallego told POLITICO. Should Pulido head to D.C. next year, he’d be joining alongside a crop of fresh progressive Democrats who have ridden the wave of democratic socialism in blue enclaves — most notably New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez. “We're not going to agree on everything,” Pulido conceded. But with Texas primed to get even more electoral votes in future presidential cycles, the party’s direction has to “resonate inside the middle of the heartland,” he said. But it’s not only electoral numbers: the early Democratic nominating calendar is heavily Latino, with both New Mexico and Nevada in the lineup. Mexican-American men could help tip the scales in either state. Pulido knows if he pulls off the win, potential 2028 hopefuls will come flocking, asking him how to win over the Rio Grande Valley. Could he see himself backing 2028 presidential candidates if he wins? They’ll have to convince Pulido first. “I will hold any type of endorsement or anything very close to my chest, and I will definitely make sure that I get behind somebody that has a policy that resonates with Hispanics,” Pulido said. Since Pulido released his hit single “Desvelado” in the mid-90s to today, his hometown of Edinburg and its sister cities across the area transformed from a once-reliable blue working class district to a part of the country deeply wary of the Democratic establishment. Latino voters have embraced the economic populism of Trump and other GOP candidates who touted their more conservative values. In 2022, De La Cruz clinched the district for Republicans. By 2024, Democrats lacked an economic message or answers for what many in the area decried as wide-open borders, Pulido told reporters on the sidelines of his rally in Mercedes on Friday. That’s made the stakes for his races all the bigger, with the RGV becoming the ultimate bellwether. “Bobby's politics are different from the way that we have branded ourselves nationally as a party, but I think that's a good thing,” said Melissa Morales of Somos PAC, which has poured millions into Pulido’s race. But Pulido’s campaign has been marred by scandal. He’s taken heat for crude social media posts about women and gay people. Frankie Caballero, one of his former bandmates, was convicted as a child sex offender . Pulido insisted he was not aware of Caballero’s history while he was in the band as a contractor, having not done a background check. Caballero was convicted in 2014, but later returned to performing with Pulido. De La Cruz’s campaign has made Pulido’s ties to Caballero a staple of attacks. “Bobby Pulido had his uncle drop a child rape charge against a friend so he could play in his band. Then he bailed this pedophile out of jail, brought him to a middle school, and looked the other way while he molested children in South Texas. Latinas are choosing Monica De La Cruz, a working mom fighting for their families, over a corrupt scumbag celebrity who will make life more expensive and already put a predator back on the streets because he likes his accordion,” James Shook, De La Cruz’s campaign manager, said in a statement. Pulido was defensive over his past, but apologized for his social media posts in an interview with POLITICO . He has given varied responses on what he knew about why Caballero went to prison. “I apologize for everything that I’ve ever joked about that offended anybody,” Pulido told POLITICO in August. “But I can’t continue to revisit every single one.” With hundreds flocking to Bert Ogden Arena to witness his final show, Pulido’s popularity has hardly dimmed because of it. Multiple voters in attendance who spoke with POLITICO said they had heard the allegations about Pulido and his accordionist, but none said that it was affecting their vote. “It’s unfortunate, but I’m not gonna hold it against Bobby,” said Joe Barrera, a musician from the Pharr-San Juan-Alamo area. Barrera, an independent, added that he’s still undecided between voting for Pulido or De La Cruz — but said he feels “it’s time for a change.” The economy and immigration dominated the reasons why voters in the crowd pledged their support for the singer. The cost of living has gotten “ re pe caro” — super expensive — Frank Trevino, a Democrat from Edinburg, told POLITICO. He and fellow Edinburg voter Felix Sandoval said they knew Pulido’s mother and remembered Bobby as a kid. “We need to support him, God help him,” Sandoval said. Pulido’s final show Saturday was the talk of Edinburg, from the hallways of the nearby inns to the post-concert stop at Whataburger. Clocking in at nearly two hours, it served as a greatest hits replay for the last 30 years of his life — and a trip down memory lane for many of the voters who grew up with him. “Of course I’m emotional, but I’m leaving with no regrets,” Pulido said from the stage. Pulido is simultaneously up for yet another Latin Grammy recognition this year. And for his status as a longtime entertainer, Pulido is not a fan of the comparisons to Trump, who in his words, is “full of shit.” Yet it’s also something his campaign has been (perhaps ironically) leaning into, with “Make Quinceñeras Great Again” hats nodding to what’s become his signature campaign move. With early voting kicking off on Monday, Pulido sharpened his closing pitch: He’s not for Democrats or Republicans — he’s for his district. “I want to give something back to the place that’s given me so much,” Pulido said. “And if you give me the honor of representing you in Congress, I give you my word that I’ll never forget where I came from.”
articles.headline: Democrats’ Tejano star sings to swing South Texas

articles.body: JACKSON, Mississippi — Raphael Warnock is racing to get Democrat Scott Colom elected in deep-red Mississippi. It’s part of his bigger bet on the South. Colom, a charismatic local prosecutor, is within striking distance in the polls of unseating Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. And in the absence of more dedicated resources, Warnock himself is trying to fill the gap by directing money and donors to the race. He has raised over $500,000 directly into Colom’s campaign committee, according to a person with direct knowledge of his efforts, granted anonymity to share private details. And, over the course of four separate fundraisers, has tried to steer Senate Democrats’ top donors to the race. In April, he told attendees at a Democratic donor breakfast that he thinks the party is “sleeping on” the Mississippi contest, prompting surprised laughter from the crowd, according to a recording of the event obtained by POLITICO. “I'm going to ask you to resist the Democratic tendency to ignore the South,” he told the assembled donors. “And for our own sake, for the sake of us having a possibility of winning over time, I think we can win in Mississippi if the conditions are just right.” Warnock, who is also widely seen as a potential presidential contender, is trying to capitalize on an incredibly unfavorable midterm environment for the GOP that has put more and more traditionally red states into play. He has been criss-crossing not just Mississippi, but the broader South, to convince Democrats to expand into the region and shore up their support with Black voters ahead of 2028. The time is ripe, he said, for a “new kind of Southern strategy” — a play off of former President Richard Nixon’s plan for Republicans to best Democrats in the region in the late 1960s that capitalized on white backlash to the civil rights movement. It’s been a hard sell so far, particularly in Mississippi: Republicans control all levers of state government, and Trump handily won by 24 points in 2024. The last time Mississippians sent a Democrat to the Senate was 1982. Even though national Democrats speak highly of Colom’s candidacy, their resources to compete on an expanded Senate battleground map are already strained, and money has been prioritized in more expensive, high-profile contests like Iowa, Alaska and Maine. The half-million Warnock has raised for Colom is 15% of the $3.5 million he’s managed to raise over the cycle. It’s still a strategic move on Warnock’s part: An upset win by Colom would boost the Senator’s own profile as he continues to leave the door open to running for president. And even if Colom loses, the South is a treasure trove of delegates for 2028 — and Black voters dominate the region in Democratic primaries. Pressed whether he’s interested in the White House himself, Warnock evaded, saying he’s “trying to think and pray about the highest and best use of my skills.” “I’ve been at crossroads many times, and in the moment, I've always known what to do,” he added. Other Democrats see the work as helpful regardless of what Warnock does in 2028. “The ’28 chatter is something he will listen to, but I don't think it's something that's part of a checklist he's marching towards,” said Georgia Democratic strategist Andrew Heaton, who has worked on Warnock’s Senate campaigns. “Regardless of what happens on that front, ’28 is going to be a very busy year because — especially if he decides not to run — I think there's no question he's planning on running for the Senate again.” Free from the constraints of reelection this year, Warnock has traveled across the Carolinas, Mississippi and his Georgia home to support local candidates and pitch a vision of his party’s future that runs through the region that launched his political career. In interviews with POLITICO on the campaign trail, Warnock drew parallels between Democrats’ 2020 wins in Georgia — his own, Sen. Jon Ossoff’s and former President Joe Biden’s — and the conditions he sees emerging in the Magnolia State for Democratic growth. Those kinds of wins will disappear from the horizon if Democrats fail to invest now and in the Black voters who are core to the party’s coalition, he argued. Mississippi, where over 35% of the population is Black, would be key to the Democratic Party’s efforts to win back voters of color, as many shifted toward Trump and Republicans in 2024. Strong Democratic candidates have reached around 45% of the vote in the state in recent years, but none have been able to punch through for a victory in Mississippi, which has a long history of extremely polarized voting along racial lines. But in the wake of the Supreme Court’s decision to gut the Voting Rights Act, there are signs Black voters are surging to the polls in higher numbers — and some Democrats hope that could remake the state’s politics. “It is in the interest of the party to invest in the base and have the base understand that the party understands that these are loyal Democratic voters, and Black voters want what other voters want,” said Warnock. “They want the same kind of prosperity and opportunity that all families want.” Colom was more blunt. Asked if he equates ignoring Mississippi and its Senate race to the party ignoring Black voters, he said: “Yeah, of course, 100 percent.” Democrats have not been averse to flooding money into traditionally red states in the final stretch of the campaign, but Mississippi has not yet made it high on that list, where Colom still faces an uphill battle to close the gap with Hyde-Smith. Building out the statewide grassroots infrastructure that has proved effective in places like Georgia takes time and resources, which have yet to land in Mississippi at a significant scale this cycle. “Democrats are investing in Mississippi, but not enough. And, I think, certainly not as much as I think we should, and not as much as we could,” Warnock said in an interview between campaign stops in the state. He was in somewhat of a rush: between a fundraiser for Colom and an event with local faith leaders, Warnock wanted to visit the home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights era titan who was shot and killed in the car port of his Jackson home in 1963. “We're playing enough here to force the other side to compete in Mississippi, and that is an improvement, but it's not enough,” he said. Colom himself has begged national Democrats to focus on his race. “Mississippi has really always been competitive. It just hasn't got the attention, the resources it deserves,” Colom said in an interview at his campaign headquarters. Some has come: American Bridge, a Democrat-aligned super PAC, pumped over $2 million into the race earlier this month, and earlier this week the New York Times reported that a single megadonor is set to split $7 million of his personal wealth between Colom’s race and others. Several top Democrats have made an effort to signal their support. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg plan to visit the state before Election Day. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and his Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair, Kirsten Gillibrand, have each hosted separate fundraisers for Colom, according to a source familiar with the events, granted anonymity to share private details. And Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, a DSCC vice-chair, campaigned with Colom in Mississippi. Colom’s campaign committee outraised Hyde-Smith’s over the summer, posting $1.3 million to her just over $640,000 . But it pales in comparison to the tens of millions that have flooded into other states. In separate statements, spokespeople for the DSCC and Senate Majority PAC lauded Colom as a strong candidate, but said they were constrained by how much they could spend. Both groups said they were monitoring the race “closely.” Republicans are still publicly maintaining their confidence in their hold on the seat. Jake Monssen, Hyde-Smith’s campaign manager, tied Colom to Washington Democrats in a statement and said the campaign “planned for Colom to have plenty of resources. We are executing our own campaign plan with that in mind.” One day after his sojourn in Mississippi, Warnock was presented with a stark contrast in what Democrats are capable of when they devote resources to a Southern state. He was in North Carolina on Thursday, where Democratic Senate nominee Roy Cooper is dominating his Republican opponent , Michael Whatley, in fundraising and polling. As one of Democrats’ top candidate recruits of the cycle, Cooper has attracted significant resources and national attention from the outset of the race. But Mississippi and North Carolina are two enormously different states, in population, income, and demographics — and that change didn’t happen overnight. Democrats began significantly investing in the state ever since President Barack Obama’s 2008 victory there and ramped up their efforts after the GOP-led state government redrew the state’s congressional maps in 2013. “It's taken a lot over the last 13 years,” Rep. Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.) said on the sidelines of a party canvass kickoff in Durham. “Our eye has never been taken off the ball, and because we believe that we could make that change, that we needed to be the change that we wanted to see, we have put that in action now, and we're going to win because of it.”
articles.headline: Can Scott Colom win Mississippi Senate? Warnock is making a big bet on it.

articles.body: GIRDWOOD, Alaska — Dan Sullivan isn’t running away from President Donald Trump like so many other vulnerable Republicans. He’s betting that walking the line instead will help him reap reelection in November. During a candidate debate, speaking at an economic forum and in an interview with Playbook this week, Sullivan repeatedly denied chances to put distance between himself and Trump’s most unpopular policies and positions. Has the economic pain from the war with Iran been worth it for Alaskans? “The real economic pain is when Democrats get control,” Sullivan told POLITICO, sitting in the shadow of a well-antlered taxidermy moose head, next to a roaring fire, at a ski resort tucked up in the mountains off the Turnagain Arm southeast of Anchorage. What about the $5,000 dividends Trump has promised voters if Republicans hold control of Congress, as he did at a rally for Sullivan in Wasilla on Tuesday? “I’ve got to look at the legislation. I don't know,” Sullivan said. “That was the first time I heard it from him, and I would just evaluate that if and when it happens.” Does he want to see data centers — which Trump has pushed for further development despite some pushback from local communities — pop up on Alaska’s undeveloped land? He’s not putting his foot down. “They definitely got to pay their own way in terms of energy,” Sullivan said. “They have to have local input and approval, and we’ll see.” Still, Sullivan bristled on some issues that touch closer to home. In light of Trump’s decision to import Russian diesel, did Sullivan think the Trump administration was being too friendly with Russia? “I thought you were asking me campaign stuff,” Sullivan replied. “Is this like a hit piece or what?” “I know my view on Russia. I'm very hawkish on Russia,” Sullivan continued, pointing to an op-ed he wrote during Trump's first administration about whether the president was too close with Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I wrote an op-ed essentially saying, sometimes I don't agree with the rhetoric, but at the end of the day, what does Putin understand? He understands power. What's the ultimate source of power that the Russians fear? U.S. military power, which Republicans always build up, Democrats always cut.” Though his office put out a statement decrying the diesel move, Sullivan didn’t sign a bipartisan letter calling on the president to reverse the decision — which he said he never saw — and instead took his concerns straight to the White House. “I speak to the administration all the time on the issues of high energy costs,” Sullivan said. Art Hackney, a veteran Republican strategist in Alaska who runs a pro-Sullivan super PAC called “We Stand with Dan,” said in an interview that another part of the calculus is that Murkowski has provided a straightforward example of how Trump treats Republicans who publicly disagree with him. “If Dan did something considered a disrespectful trigger or something, what do you think would happen? It could well have implications for things that affect Alaska's economy.” But Trump, for better or worse, is a centerpiece of races like Sullivan’s. The president has pleaded with voters at rallies to “pretend I'm on the ballot” — just as he did alongside Sullivan on Tuesday. And Alaska’s tighter-than-expected Senate race is poised to be a linchpin for deciding which party holds control of the chamber. Alaska, Ohio and Iowa are the races that Trump officials view as increasingly critical to keep their majority, according to three GOP officials familiar with the Trump-aligned super PAC MAGA Inc.’s strategy, granted anonymity to candidly assess the midterms. Sullivan only sees Trump’s presence as a boon. “I think the rally certainly helps in terms of energizing the base,” Sullivan said. He’s proud to have the president campaign alongside him, plus Vice President JD Vance, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas). “I'm bringing up my people,” Sullivan said. “I’m not afraid of that.” Polls show Sullivan tied with or trailing former Rep. Mary Peltola, one of Democrats’ top hopes to help flip the Senate. On paper, this contest shouldn’t be close: Peltola lost her House seat after just one term. “It was Trump plus-13 two years ago, so it is not the position we’d love to be in, but we’re doing what we do to help get him across the finish line,” said Kevin Greene, the state director for Americans for Prosperity-Alaska, which has knocked on tens of thousands of doors for Sullivan. On one such door-to-door trip with Greene in Anchorage on Thursday morning, voters across approximately a dozen houses were about evenly split between supporting Sullivan or Peltola. Only one agreed to speak on the record to POLITICO: John Baker, a 67-year-old retiree who said he used to be a Republican but would be supporting Peltola this year. What happened? “Donald Trump happened,” Baker said. He added that his support for Peltola was 70% because he wanted to see Democrats take the Senate and 30% because he liked her as a candidate. Peltola, the first Alaska Native to represent the state in Congress, has centered her campaign around “fish, family, and freedom” while capitalizing on voters’ frustrations with the high cost of energy and goods, particularly in remote communities. She has focused on outreach to villages in the Alaskan bush and has largely shied away from national attention, including from the media. The former congresswoman has some major liabilities that Sullivan often slams. Just two years ago, she lost her reelection bid after only one full term. She has sought to distance herself from the Biden administration, which remains unpopular in the state. She has a reputation for missing meetings and votes. And a New York Times report last month alleged that she created a hostile work environment and regularly used slurs and other offensive language. Even those close to her campaign, though optimistic, acknowledge it’s still an uphill battle. “It’s always been long odds,” said John-Henry Heckendorn, a Democratic strategist in Alaska whose firm is supporting Peltola outside of her official campaign. Peltola, he said, would have to do about twice as well as the Democratic Senate challengers in the past four cycles in order to win. At the debate on Thursday, Peltola said she “prided” herself on being “available to Alaskan press” — though she acknowledged she has “really demurred from national attention, from national outlets.” After the debate, POLITICO asked Peltola: “You said you’re accessible to the press. Will you take some questions?” She smiled, then walked away quickly, with an aide saying she had a dinner to attend. “She’s hoping that the Joe Biden bunker mentality will win, and you know, maybe it will,” Sullivan told POLITICO on Friday. “I don't think it will. I think Alaskans can see through it.” Peltola’s campaign declined several interview requests for this story. In an email to POLITICO, the campaign noted that Sullivan was in the top quarter of most-absent senators , and that Peltola had to miss congressional votes when both her husband and mother died. The email also noted that Peltola helped secure the Willow oil-drilling project and has a record of bucking her fellow Democrats. Peltola has hosted at least 16 events in Alaska this month, the campaign said, and has interviewed with eight news outlets in the past week. “Dan Sullivan has tripled his wealth in the Senate and voted fourteen times for the war in Iran that is raising costs one everything from gas to groceries, Mary has been talking with Alaskans in every corner of the state about her plan to take on the rigged system in DC, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Harry Child, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to POLITICO. Sullivan is leaning on his strong legislative record and support for oil and gas development in the state. He has sought to tie Peltola to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Joe Biden and Kamala Harris, and has attributed her massive fundraising edge to “lower-48 liberal millionaires and billionaires who want to turn Alaska into national parks.” Though he’s largely embracing Trump, there’s still moments of disagreement. But even in those spaces, he’s touting his close ties to the White House and effectiveness as a Washington operator instead of pushing the president away. Sullivan was opposed to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of the convicted Fort Hood shooter, and told POLITICO “there’s probably no senator weighing in more with senior White House and directly with the Secretary of War than me, saying this is not a good idea.” Trump called off the livestream on Thursday . Trump’s approval rating here, like the country at large, is underwater. The war with Iran has hit Alaska hard, where nearly all goods are imported by plane or barge, with urban gas prices hovering around $5 per gallon and prices in the bush often double that. In a year when Republican voters may be more likely to stay home without Trump on the ballot — Democrats eye an opening. “We have a golden opportunity with a fantastic candidate on our end and a really mediocre one on theirs,” said Alaska Democratic Party Chair Eric Croft. “I think we've been coming that way for a long time, and this is our chance to pump through.” Trump on Tuesday flew more than eight hours from Washington to Wasilla, home of Sarah Palin and the Iditarod, with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, FCC Chair Brendan Carr and FHFA Administrator Bill Pulte in tow. He announced that Taiwan had joined South Korea in its commitments to a proposed Alaska energy pipeline — though the project is still in flux — and that the FCC will vote this month to invest an additional $162 million to expand high-speed internet in the state. Thousands of the president’s fans piled into the ice hockey rink and thousands more gathered outside, watching Trump speak on a jumbotron. Asked by POLITICO what he thought about Peltola, rally attendee Jeff Caswell, 59, replied: “I don’t.” But in a state where independents outnumber Republicans, that enthusiasm may only go so far. “Very conservative MAGA voters can’t vote for you harder,” said Scott Kendall, a veteran political strategist who worked on two of Alaska GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s campaigns and was chief of staff to former Alaska Gov. Bill Walker. “Donald Trump’s support in this current climate is both a blessing and a curse,” Kendall noted. Even some reliable Trump supporters at the rally acknowledged the outlook appeared bleak. “I think Alaska’s turning blue,” Matt Niessink, a 45-year-old general contractor from Wasilla, said at the rally. He said he had voted for Trump three times and planned to support Republicans this year. What did he wish the president would do differently? “I wish he’d shut his mouth sometimes and not be such a pompous ass,” Niessink said.

articles.body: El Barcelona Universitari Club ha debutat aquest diumenge amb una desfeta a la Guinardera davant el Sant Cugat (38-6) . El partit ha significat l’estrena del conjunt dirigit per Aroa González , que no va poder jugar a la primera jornada, davant l’ Olímpico de Pozuelo . El duel ha estat marcat pel context de complexitat que viu el BUC en l’àmbit extraesportiu . El club ha format part d’una batalla legal per ocupar la plaça que, per mèrits esportius, havia aconseguit el Barça, però per irregularitats no va poder optar-hi . Inicialment, la plaça només la va sol·licitar el BUC, però més tard també la volia el Pozuelo. Després de tot l’enrenou, sembla que la solució és que la Lliga Iberdrola tindrà un equip més que habitualment i passa així dels vuit als nou . El fet de ser imparells provocarà que cada setmana un dels conjunts haurà de descansar. COMUNICAT OFICIAL BARCELONA UNIVERSITARI CLUB #SOMBUC #SOMCLUB pic.twitter.com/U2EwgqMU7H — BUC Rugby (@buc1929) October 8, 2026 Aquesta situació l’ha privat, fins a la setmana passada , de conèixer amb garanties si podria formar part de la Lliga Iberdrola de rugbi. Per aquest fet, les barcelonines no han pogut fer pretemporada , condicionades per la incertesa de no saber si podrien ocupar la plaça de la màxima categoria estatal. Ramon Salinas, president del BUC: “Fins dijous passat no vam saber si jugaríem a Primera Divisió” El president del BUC, Ramon Salinas, ha desgranat la situació del club i ha explicat com no han pogut planificar la temporada amb normalitat . Salinas també ha afegit que no han pogut disputar cap amistós i que “ l’objectiu de l’entitat és estar consolidat en la màxima categoria l’any del centenari del club “, el 2029. En la mateixa línia que el president, Lucía Hernández ha confessat com s’han viscut al vestidor unes circumstàncies tan insòlites. La jugadora del BUC no ha tingut pèls a la llengua per descriure la situació: “ Ha estat un caos, no sabíem ni on ni quan jugaríem, però l’objectiu és gaudir “. articles.body: La tasca de la Guàrdia Urbana de Barcelona de control i regulació del trànsit és potser la més coneguda. El que no tothom sap és que el cos disposa de dues unitats especialitzades en aquest àmbit, la Unitat Central de Trànsit (UCT) i la Unitat Central d’Atestats de Trànsit (UCAT) , totes dues amb seu a la comissaria de la Zona Franca. Una moto de la UCT s’adreça a un sinsitre a les ronda del Litoral En el tercer episodi de ‘Torn de guàrdia’ acompanyem agents de totes dues unitats. Veiem com els motoristes de la UCT són els primers en arribar als sinistres a les rondes de Barcelona per la seva capacitat de circular entre vehicles. La seva rapidesa és clau per reduir les retencions en aquestes vies principals d’accés i sortida de Barcelona. També pugem en un vehicle camuflat per copsar les principals infraccions al volant i assistim a controls de mercaderies perilloses i de llicències de VTC. La UCAT investiga les causes dels accidents més greus A ‘Sobre l’asfalt’ assistim, també, a una actuació de la UCAT en un accident en què una moto va atropellar una vianant. La unitat s’especialitza en la investigació dels accidents i delictes relacionats amb la seguretat viària a la ciutat. Parla amb testimonis, analitza càmeres, comprova les fases semafòriques, fotografia el lloc del sinistre… També és l’única unitat de la Guàrdia Urbana que disposa de calabossos i que posa a disposició judicial a presumptes autors de delictes contra la seguretat viària. Els calabossos de la UCAT per als detinguts per casos de seguretat viària es troben a la comissaria de la Zona Franca

articles.body: El Sant Andreu jugarà, el pròxim dimarts 27 d’octubre al Congost, contra el Manresa a la Copa del Rei . El que hauria de ser un bon partit de futbol català quedarà tacat pel preu excessiu en la venda d’entrades destinades al conjunt visitant. El Manresa ha fixat que cada aficionat del conjunt quadribarrat haurà de pagar 20 € per veure el partit . Diferents penyes andreuenques han mostrat el seu rebuig i es neguen a desplaçar-se per presenciar el duel. articles.body: La tardor del 1959, al centre de Ginebra, un tramvia va estar a punt d’endur-se la vida d’una de les escriptores catalanes més traduïdes: Mercè Rodoreda . L’accident hauria pogut privar la literatura catalana d’algunes de les seves obres més importants, com La plaça del Diamant , que l’autora va començar a escriure durant els mesos posteriors a l’accident, mentre es recuperava. Ara, la periodista i escriptora Eva Comas-Arnal (Gavà, 1975) publica Nit blava a Ginebra , una novel·la que pren aquest episodi com a punt de partida per explorar els anys més fructífers de l’escriptora barcelonina. “Per mi és un fet important que, just abans que Rodoreda es posés a escriure l’obra més important de les lletres catalanes , patís un accident de gravetat”, explica Comas-Arnal. Un accident gairebé desconegut Fins fa poc, l’accident del tramvia havia passat desapercebut. El 2024, Quim Torra va publicar una biografia de Joan Prat (Armand Obiols) , company sentimental de Rodoreda durant prop de 30 anys. Per documentar-la, va trobar l’agenda d’Obiols, en què anotava les activitats que feia cada dia. Aquest document va permetre reconstruir l’episodi i situar-lo en el temps. “L’accident té lloc just setmanes abans que Mercè Rodoreda es posi a escriure La plaça del Diamant , perquè està estudiat que va començar a escriure-la pels volts de Nadal del 1959 ”, explica l’escriptora. Comas-Arnal també ha descobert que el metge que va atendre Rodoreda durant la convalescència va llegir la novel·la i li va enviar una carta per felicitar-la. L’endemà, l’escriptora li va fer arribar un ram de roses vermelles. També et pot interessar La plaça del Diamant, la inspiració de Mercè Rodoreda Gabriela Grífol Porta 2 minuts de lectura Una novel·la entre Ginebra i Barcelona Nit blava a Ginebra transcorre entre la dècada dels 60, a Ginebra, i el segle XXI, a Barcelona. El protagonista és un home que es planteja escriure un llibre sobre Mercè Rodoreda, però que no és cap especialista en la seva obra. Per acostar-lo a l’univers de l’escriptora, Comas-Arnal li crea un personatge proper en l’àmbit acadèmic . “El primer que vaig veure és que no volia que fos especialista en Rodoreda, però necessitava que, d’alguna manera, tingués Rodoreda a la vora. Per tant, vaig crear-li una exdona que estava a punt de llegir la tesi doctoral sobre les obres perdudes de Mercè Rodoreda”, explica. Una mirada crítica a l’acadèmia Eva Comas-Arnal és professora universitària a la Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona i experta en l’obra de Rodoreda. A la novel·la també s’hi intueix una mirada crítica cap a determinades dinàmiques de l’acadèmia literària i dels estudis universitaris. “He de dir que l’Autònoma és un lloc meravellós, és la millor universitat on he fet classe mai. Però també t’he de dir que he fet classes a moltes altres universitats i, de vegades, hi he trobat actituds i maneres de fer que no afavoreixen el coneixement . I això sí que crec que és criticable”, afirma. Davant d’aquestes dinàmiques, l’autora reivindica el gaudi i la llibertat personal: “Jo el que intento fer és gaudir moltíssim i agafar una frase de Rodoreda que aquesta no me la trauran, que és allunyar-me de tot allò que em faci mal”. També et pot interessar Maruja Torres: “Ser feliç és la millor venjança, malgrat tot” Víctor Giralt Jonama 2 minuts de lectura La mirada, les mans i el somriure de Rodoreda Més enllà de la seva obra literària, la imatge de Mercè Rodoreda també ha perdurat en l’imaginari col·lectiu. Quan li preguntem què li crida més l’atenció de l’escriptora, Comas-Arnal ho té clar: “A mi, de la imatge de Rodoreda, el que sempre em crida més l’atenció són els ulls: una mirada amb molta curiositat i amb una gran capacitat de mirar l’ànima humana. Ella sempre diu que li agradava molt mirar”. L’autora també destaca les mans, perquè a Rodoreda li encantava tocar, igual que a molts dels seus personatges. I, finalment, el somriure: “Ràpidament està a punt de convertir-se en una riallada d’aquelles que feia sovint”. Mercè Rodoreda

articles.body: Les escoles i instituts ja fa anys que són testimonis de les onades migratòries viscudes els últims anys. Cada vegada més alumnes d’arreu del món arriben als centres i necessiten una atenció més personalitzada: per aprendre la llengua, però també per integrar-se en un entorn completament nou. A Barcelona hi ha 246 aules d’acollida . Una d’aquestes es troba a l’institut Icària, que ja fa més de 10 anys que té aquest espai per garantir l’aprenentatge intensiu del català, dels coneixements bàsics i la incorporació progressiva de l’alumnat a l’aula ordinària. “L’aula d’acollida ens ajuda a integrar aquest alumnat perquè segueixi els estudis d’una manera eficaç i que pugui sortir de l’institut amb un nivell acceptable”, explica Àlvar Martín, director de l’institut . També et pot interessar El nou curs escolar 2026-27, a punt: més professors, rècord d’aules d’acollida i límits a la IA Redacció 3 minuts de lectura “Ens han ajudat molt” Per als alumnes aquest recurs es converteix en un espai de referència que els permet sentir-se més a gust i amb confiança a l’institut. “He començat a parlar català molt bé, escriure i llegir. Ara sé moltes coses que altres alumnes o companys no saben”, explica l ‘Umme , de Pakistán, que va arribar a l’institut fa tres anys. A la Suri, de Colòmbia, també li agrada molt poder dedicar unes hores a l’aula d’acollida que assegura que li ha faciltat poder conversar amb els companys. “La Pilar (la tutora) és com si fos una mare per mi perquè sempre està per nosaltres i ens ha ajudat molt”, afegeix. Cada aula d’acollida té assignada un tutor o tutora que és qui s’encarrega de planificar el curs, tenint en compte les necessitats de cada un dels alumnes i aplicant les metodologies d’immersió lingüística , i estratègies d’inclusió social . La Pilar Poy , tutora de l’aula d’acollida de l’institut Icària, explica que es posa el focus en els aspectes emocionals: “És molt important aquesta vessant més social i emocional perquè això també ajuda que ells vulguin aprendre una llengua nova i s’integrin amb més facilitat dins de l’entorn dels seus iguals”. A mesura que han anat transcorrent els minuts, els quadribarrats s’han anat sentint més còmodes. Tovar ha tingut la primera i Torices ha desaprofitat un mà a mà. La igualtat a l’electrònic ha durat ben poc, ja que Alexis ha servit un córner ràpid i Bermejo ha tornat a avançar al conjunt de Natxo González . A partir d’aquí, el Sant Andreu ha intentat sentenciar el partit amb un Alexis García molt inspirat. L’alegria s’ha acabat al tram final quan l’àrbitre ha xiulat un penal molt dubtós a favor dels visitants. Cristian Rodríguez l’ha transformat i ha empatat. El mateix criteri, però, no s’ha mantingut més tard, quan Alexis ha caigut dins l’àrea desestabilitzat per un defensor.

articles.body: El novembre d’aquest any, o sigui, el mes que ve, s’havia de començar a implementar a l’estat espanyol el sistema de dipòsit, devolució i retorn per als envasos de plàstic (SDDR). Es tracta de tota una revolució en el món del reciclatge que permet recuperar el 90% dels envasos de begudes . Actualment a l’estat espanyol només se’n recuperen un 41.3% i se n’abandonen 35 milions cada dia. La posada en marxa del projecte va amb retard , però des de l’ONG Retorna, esperen que el sistema de retorn sigui una realitat el gener de 2028 . Com es farà aquesta recollida? Els envasos es podran retornar tant en grans superficies com en petits establiments . “Com ja passa en 19 països de tot Europa i és un èxit, quan vas a comprar, portes els teus envasos buits , les llaunes i les ampolles i quan passes per caixa, te’ls compten i t’ho descompten de la compra o et donen els diners . A les grans superfícies poden escollir, perquè hi ha fabricants que ofereixen maquinària per fer això de manera automàtica . Tu vas allà, poses els teus envasos i et tornen els diners o et donen un tiquet que després et descomptaran a la caixa. Pel consumidor és un èxit ” ha explicat a l’ Infobarris el director de l’ONG Retorna, Miquel Roset. Per què s’ha d’implementar el sistema de dipòsit? Deixant de banda si s’està a favor o no del reciclatge i de salvar el planeta, hi ha una normativa europea que ho diu ben clar: El Reglament sobre envasos i residus d’envasos (PPWR en anglès) obliga als estats membres a recuperar selectivament el 90% de totes les ampolles de plàstic i llaunes de begudes l’any 2029 . Cada país ho pot fer com vulgui, ja sigui amb el contenidor groc o amb el sistema de dipòsit si el té. Actualment Espanya està recuperant el 41.3% , per això la Llei de Residus aprovada l’abril de 2022, especifica que s’ha de posar en marxa el SDDR a l’estat espanyol, ja que amb el sistema de contenidors actual no es pot assolir la recuperació que marca Europa. Quins països europeus ja han implementat el SDDR? 19 països europeus ja han implementat el sistema de dipòsit, devolució i retorn per als envasos de plàstic. Dels 27 països de la Unió Europea ho han fet 17: Suècia va ser el primer país que ho va posar en marxa fa 42 anys, el 1996 ho va fer Finlàndia, després Dinamarca el 2002, Alemanya el 2003, Estònia el 2005, Croàcia i Països Baixos el 2006, Lituània el 2016, Eslovàquia, Letònia i Malta el 2022, Romania el 2023, Irlanda i Hongria el 2024, Àustria i Polònia el 2025 i Portugal el 2026 . Islàndia i Noruega, que no pertanyen a la UE, també ho van implementar el 1989 i el 1999, respectivament. Ciutats més netes amb el sistema de dipòsit El que s’ha observat en els països on s’ha implementat el sistema de retorn és que té un efecte positiu no només amb els envasos, sinó també en la neteja de totes les ciutats . “Si no veus envasos tirats a terra, descuidats, la gent ens comporta de forma més cívica , si un lloc està brut ja, a la gent li és igual” explica Roset. “Ho vam veure a Cadaqués on es va fer una prova pilot l’any 2013, i ho estem veient a Portugal on han triplicat els envasos que recuperen en només 6 mesos , cosa que no havien fet en 30 anys. Amb la implementació d’aquest sistema es crea com una espiral positiva , i això és el que arribarà d’aquí 14 o 15 mesos a casa nostra : evitarem que aquests 35 milions de llaunes, ampolles i brics acabin enterrats, cremats o perduts per la Diagonal, per un camí a la platja de la Marbella o a sota un banc de la plaça Catalunya” conclou.
